1. Poetry becomes acceptable by virtue of ornamentation—
Poetry becomes acceptable by virtue of its ornaments.
In reality, the term "poetry" applies to such words and subjects.

While "matter" (*artha*) is commonly understood as that which is adorned or beautified by *śabda* (diction or qualities of style) and *alaṃkāra* (embellishments), in the present context it is used in its secondary and much wider sense, denoting both "word" (*śabda*) and "subject-matter" (*vastu*).
Regarding "matter" without any qualification,
note that here poetry is defined primarily as "such words and subject-matter as are beautified by diction and figures of speech," and secondarily as mere words.
And "subject matter. Older writers have declared that poetry has "word" as its body and "subject matter" as its soul;
however, the author of this [work] adds that the subject matter should be such as is relished by those with poetic sensibility.
Later writers, among them the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*,

have described poetry as a living being whose body consists of "word" (*śabda*) and "meaning" (*artha*), whose soul consists of the excellences of suggestion or implication (*vyañjanā-guṇa*), and whose ornaments consist of the poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*).

Ornaments. The author of the *Tattvaviveka* defines poetry as "such words and subject matter as are free from all defects and adorned by style (*rīti*)," and he does not consider the presence of "figures of speech" (*alaṃkāra*) to be a necessary element; in this regard, [he differs from others].

It has the support of [the *Kāvyaprakāśa*], which declares: "Even when adorned by figures of speech, poetry would not be poetry if it lacked *rīti* (diction) or *guṇa* (quality of style). Thus, according to these [authorities], the "absence of defects" enters only as a negative property (*paryudāsa*) of poetry.

Writers must possess some excellent subject matter expressed in words capable of conveying the intended meaning; furthermore, that meaning should be merely suggested and not directly expressed— this is not, at least according to many writers, a necessary requirement.
It has been established as the condition for the first class of poetry alone.

With all this in view, the *Tattvakaumudī* has defined poetry as "that word which expresses an elegant subject matter" (*sādhu-vastu-abhidhāyaka-śabdaḥ*), and this accords with what [the author] stated.
Dhvani has stated that with respect to poetry, the word is the body and the meaning intended by a sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) is the soul.
What, then, is an "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*)?
